corpus.title: UniCAS: A foundation model for cervical cytology screening
corpus.authors: Haotian Jiang et al.
corpus.modality: Cervical cytology whole-slide images (WSI) from ThinPrep Cytology Test (TCT), 20x magnification
corpus.methodology: Vision Transformer (ViT) foundation model pretrained with DINOv2 self-supervised learning over ~1 million steps on unlabeled cytology patches. Downstream uses a multi-task aggregator combining task-specific attention and a Task Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) for concurrent slide-level diagnosis; linear probing for region-level classification; ViTDet for detection/segmentation; DA-CLIP for pixel-level image enhancement.
corpus.novelty: First cytology-specific (rather than histopathology) foundation model for cervical screening; unified multi-scale analysis spanning slide-, region-, and pixel-levels; multi-task aggregator that performs several slide-level diagnoses concurrently while cutting diagnostic time ~70% and pipeline 3x faster.
corpus.training_datasets: Confirmed as stated. Self-supervised pretraining on 48,532 cervical WSIs (80,314,640 patches; 34,103 NILM normal and 14,429 abnormal cases; patients aged 15-90). Downstream training sets: cancer screening 28,110 WSIs (split 19,894 train / 2,210 val / 6,006 test), candidiasis 1,506 WSIs, clue cell 3,616 WSIs, subtype diagnosis 970 WSIs (NILM 200, ASC-US 200, LSIL 200, ASC-H 200, HSIL 170), plus region-level annotation sets.
corpus.eval_datasets: Confirmed as stated. Internal held-out test splits; external multi-center cohort of 2,304 WSIs = 2,129 WSIs from six previously unseen scanning devices + 175 additional WSIs collected January 2025. Public benchmarks: BMT, Herlev, SIPaKMeD, ComparisonDetector, ISBI 2014, CNSeg, Cx22-Multi. Explicit external/cross-dataset validation performed.
corpus.evaluation_results: Confirmed as stated. Slide-level multi-task aggregator: cancer AUC 92.60%, candidiasis AUC 92.58%, clue cell AUC 98.39%. External validation: cancer AUC 90.10%, candidiasis AUC 89.92%, clue cell AUC 98.11%. Region-level (linear probing) F1: cervical abnormality 91.47%, candidiasis 96.30%, clue cells 98.44%. Public benchmarks: Herlev F1 96.02%; SIPaKMeD F1 97.73%; BMT AUC 99.19% NILM / 98.54% LSIL / 99.79% HSIL. Segmentation Dice: ISBI 2014 92.11% average (cytoplasm 92.99%, nuclei 91.23%), CNSeg 90.69%, Cx22-Multi 94.38%. Efficiency 9.75 s/WSI.
corpus.gaps: Fixed-scale processing (no multi-magnification); no histopathological gold-standard validation (cytology-only labels); no LLM integration for interpretability/NL interaction; limited coverage of rare entities outside training; needs prospective multi-institutional clinical validation.
corpus._evidence: "Our multi-task aggregator finishes slide-level screening in just 9.75 s per WSI"; multi-task aggregator "AUC values of 92.60%" (cancer), "92.58%" (candidiasis), "98.39%" (clue cell); external "AUCs of 90.10%" / "89.92%" / "98.11%"; "2,129 WSIs from six previously unseen scanning devices and 175 additional WSIs collected in January 2025, forming a comprehensive external test set of 2,304 WSIs."
corpus._verify_notes: All claims verified against the PMC source (PMC12866161), which is the open-access version of the Cell Reports Medicine article (DOI 10.1016/j.xcrm.2025.102570). Title, full author list (Haotian Jiang, Jiangdong Cai, Zhenrong Shen, Mengjie Xu, Manman Fei, Haolin Huang, Xinyu Wang, Rui Bi, Dinggang Shen, Lichi Zhang, Qian Wang), year (2026), and venue all match. Every reported metric, training dataset size, and evaluation dataset detail matches the source verbatim, including the 9.75 s/WSI efficiency figure, the 970-WSI subtype set, and the external cohort breakdown (2,129 + 175 = 2,304 WSIs across six unseen scanners). Minor clarification: the region-level F1 scores are reported under the "linear probing" evaluation protocol; pretraining data was collected from 11 scanning devices (May 2022-Nov 2023) across diverse geographic regions, though the exact number of regions is not quantified. No discrepancies or fabricated numbers found.

corpus.title: Federated Learning for Histopathology Image Classification: A Systematic Review
corpus.authors: Meriem Touhami, Mohammad Faizal Ahmad Fauzi, Zaka Ur Rehman, Sarina Mansor
corpus.modality: Histopathology / whole-slide pathology image classification (multi-cancer; survey)
corpus.methodology: Systematic review (PRISMA-style) of 24 studies (2020-2025) on federated learning for histopathology image classification. Catalogs aggregation algorithms (FedAvg in 14/24 studies, plus FedProx, FedDropoutAvg, and custom methods FedDBL, FedImp, SiloBN, FedSAF, HarmoFL), model architectures (VGG, ResNet, DenseNet, EfficientNet), datasets, FL frameworks, and non-IID / privacy handling strategies. Notes knowledge-distillation-based methods: FedDBL (bidirectional knowledge distillation, weighted averaging) and FedWSIDD (dataset-distillation aggregation with synthetic slides).
corpus.novelty: First comprehensive systematic review focused specifically on federated learning for histopathology image classification, consolidating datasets, frameworks, aggregation strategies, non-IID handling, and privacy approaches, and exposing inconsistent reporting standards across the field.
corpus.training_datasets: Confirmed. Survey-level (not a single model). The review reports 10 datasets used across studies: 8 public, 1 private, 1 unspecified. The named public datasets include BreakHis, TCGA, Camelyon16/17, LC25000, HAM10000, MC-CRC, PanNuke, and MedMNIST.
corpus.eval_datasets: Confirmed. Same public histopathology datasets are used for evaluation per reviewed study. The review notes limited robustness/validation across institutions with extreme domain shift and emphasizes the need for validation across multi-institutional clinical environments.
corpus.evaluation_results: Confirmed. Across the 24 reviewed studies (2020-2025), classification accuracies range from 69.37% to 99.72%. FedAvg was the most commonly used aggregation algorithm in 14 of 24 studies. Only 2 studies explicitly reported their FL framework (Flower and OpenFL). This is a review-level synthesis with no single headline metric.
corpus.gaps: Identifies field-wide gaps: lack of standardized evaluation protocols, limited real-world multi-institutional validation, insufficient testing under extreme heterogeneity and client dropout, under-reporting of FL frameworks, and need for better interpretability and robustness under severe inter-site staining/hardware variability.

corpus.title: TopotiCerv: Multimodal classification of cervical lesions using acetowhite colposcopic images and clinical findings
corpus.authors: Chandra Das, et al.
corpus.modality: Multimodal: post-acetic-acid (acetowhite) colposcopy images + structured clinical/tabular findings (HPV status, squamocolumnar junction visibility, transformation zone type, acetic-acid uptake)
corpus.methodology: Segmentation-free pipeline. Pretrained CNN backbones (DenseNet121/169, EfficientNetV2-S/B3, Xception, MobileNetV2) fine-tuned via transfer learning with smoothed class weights and a hybrid loss; clinical variables one-hot encoded and normalized. Fusion strategies compared: early, intermediate, late, attention-based, and a compact Transformer-based fusion (best). Temperature scaling for probability calibration; rigorous augmentation and fairness checks. Three-class output: Normal, Precancerous, Cancerous. DenseNet121 reported as strongest image backbone.
corpus.novelty: Addresses the gap of jointly modeling acetowhite-specific visual patterns with structured clinical variables; proposes a compact Transformer-based multimodal fusion with calibration and fairness checks for early triage in resource-constrained settings using IARC/WHO data.
corpus.training_datasets: Confirmed. Dataset sourced from the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) under WHO, comprising post-acetic-acid colposcopy images with matched clinical variables. Exact sample size and train/val/test splits not reported in accessible (indexed) sources.
corpus.eval_datasets: Confirmed. Evaluated on the IARC/WHO colposcopy dataset (held-out internal evaluation). No external/cross-dataset validation reported in accessible sources.
corpus.evaluation_results: Confirmed. Transformer-based fusion model: AUC-ROC ~0.999, AUC-PR ~0.999, accuracy ~0.98, MCC 0.978, Cohen's kappa 0.977, well-calibrated probabilities after temperature scaling, 3-class (Normal/Precancerous/Cancerous). DenseNet121 reported as best visual backbone. Fusion strategies compared: Early, Intermediate, Late, Attention-based, Transformer-based.

corpus.authors: Harmanpreet Kaur, Reecha Sharma, Jagroop Kaur
corpus.modality: Pap-smear cytology single-cell images
corpus.methodology: Benchmark of 16 ImageNet-pretrained CNNs via transfer learning (VGG16/19; ResNet50/50V2/101/101V2/152/152V2; DenseNet121/169/201; MobileNet; XceptionNet; InceptionV3; InceptionResNetV2). Frozen conv layers + fine-tuned head (Global Average Pooling, BatchNorm, Dropout, Dense, SoftMax). corpus.title: CausalCervixNet: convolutional neural networks with causal insight (CICNN) in cervical cancer cell classification—leveraging deep learning models for enhanced diagnostic accuracy
corpus.authors: Zahra Taghados, Zohreh Azimifar, Malihezaman Monsefi, Mojgan Akbarzadeh Jahromi
corpus.venue: BMC Cancer, 25:607 (Springer Nature / BioMed Central); DOI 10.1186/s12885-025-13926-2
corpus.modality: Cervical cytopathology Pap-smear microscopic cell images
corpus.methodology: Causal-insight CNN (CICNN): transfer-learning backbones (VGG16, VGG19, ResNet50, XceptionNet; best = CICNN-ResNet50) augmented with causal discovery/inference — Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC), Kernel Conditional Independence Test (KCIT), and causality maps of pairwise conditional probabilities between features. corpus.novelty: Integrates causal discovery, causal reasoning and causal inference into a CNN diagnostic framework to uncover hidden causal factors in cervical cell images (interpretability) rather than relying on correlations alone.
corpus.training_datasets: Confirmed as stated. SIPaKMeD (4,049 cells, 5 classes; 16,982 augmented training images, ~6x), ShUCSEIT self-collected (2,201 cells, 5 classes; 9,240 augmented), Herlev (917 cells, 7 classes; 8,190 augmented, ~14x); split 60% train / 20% val / 20% test.

corpus.title: Deep learning models for cervical cancer subtyping using whole slide images
corpus.authors: Hai-yan Yan, Xiao-ping Shen, Pin-pin Tao, Lei Jin, Yu-lan Zhang, Mei Wang
corpus.modality: Cervical histopathology H&E-stained whole-slide images (WSI)
corpus.methodology: Two-tier strategy: patch-level classification with four CNNs (AlexNet, VGG19, ResNet-50, Inception-v3), then WSI-level aggregation via multiple-instance learning using TF-IDF and histogram features fed to classical classifiers (logistic regression, random forest, SVM, AdaBoost, XGBoost). corpus.title: Multimodal deep learning model for prognostic prediction in cervical cancer receiving definitive radiotherapy: a multi-center study (CerviPro)
corpus.authors: Weiping Wang, Guang Yang, Yulin Liu, et al.
corpus.venue: npj Digital Medicine (Nature Portfolio / Nature Publishing Group)
corpus.modality: Multimodal: pre- and post-treatment pelvic CT imaging + handcrafted radiomics + clinical/tabular variables (age, FIGO stage, tumor size, hemoglobin, SCC antigen, lymph node metastasis status)
corpus.methodology: 3D U-Net for automatic tumor segmentation (eliminating manual ROI delineation); deep features (8192) from a pretrained foundation model reduced to 30 PCA components; 214 handcrafted radiomic features narrowed to 147 via variance-based selection; 9 clinical variables; multi-layer perceptron (MLP) for multimodal feature fusion; DeepHit-based survival prediction framework for disease-free survival (DFS).
corpus.novelty: Integrates BOTH pre- and post-treatment CT (capturing post-treatment tumor dynamics) with automated segmentation and multimodal fusion of imaging, radiomics and clinical data to predict DFS in locally advanced cervical cancer treated with definitive radiotherapy; addresses limitations of single-timepoint radiomics and manual ROI delineation.
corpus.training_datasets: Confirmed. Training cohort: 691 patients (Peking Union Medical College Hospital). Internal validation: 173 patients (same institution). Total cohort 1,018 patients across all sites.
corpus.eval_datasets: Confirmed. Internal validation cohort (n=173, Peking Union Medical College Hospital). Two external sites: Xijing Hospital (n=55) and The Second Affiliated Hospital of Dalian Medical University (n=99). External/cross-dataset validation: Yes.
corpus.evaluation_results: Confirmed. Internal validation (n=173): C-index 0.806; time-dependent AUC 0.79/0.80/0.80 at 12/36/60 months; KM p<0.001. External cohort 1 (Xijing, n=55): AUC ~0.64/0.63 at the reported timepoints; KM p=0.085 (not significant). External cohort 2 (Dalian, n=99): KM p=0.211 (not significant). Training cohort (n=691): AUC 0.96/0.92/0.87. Transfer-learning fine-tuning on 20% of external data improved external AUC to 0.76-0.79 (p<0.001); retraining raised 12-month AUC from 0.64 to 0.70 and external C-index from 0.662 to 0.700. Abstract reports external C-index 0.70 & 0.66.
corpus.gaps: Reduced external-validation performance attributed to patient-characteristic differences, imaging-protocol variation, and shorter follow-up; limited long-term (60-month) accuracy; no systematic exploration of CT acquisition parameters (slice thickness, reconstruction); no molecular/pathological biomarkers; single imaging modality (CT only); black-box interpretability concerns.

corpus.title: Machine Learning for Preoperative Assessment and Postoperative Prediction in Cervical Cancer: Multicenter Retrospective Model Integrating MRI and Clinicopathological Data
corpus.authors: Shuqi Li, Chenyan Guo, Yufei Fang, Junjun Qiu, He Zhang, Lei Ling, Jie Xu, Xinwei Peng, Chuchu Jiang, Jue Wang, Keqin Hua
corpus.modality: Multimodal: coronal T2-weighted fat-suppressed pelvic contrast-enhanced MRI + clinicopathological/tabular data (preoperative: age, comorbidity, HPV status, SCC antigen, LEEP history; postoperative: 21 parameters incl. FIGO stage, tumor size, histologic type, depth of stromal invasion, LVSI, surgical margins, keratinization, differentiation, P53/P16/Ki-67)
corpus.methodology: 3D U-Net with squeeze-and-excitation layer for lesion segmentation; image normalization, min-max scaling for continuous variables, one-hot encoding for categoricals; improved Focal Loss (alpha=0.25, gamma=2) for class imbalance. Fusion by concatenating clinical feature vectors (5-D preoperative; 57-D postoperative) with a 65,536-D image vector to form 65,593-D integrated vectors. Seven ML classifiers tested: KNN, SVM, decision tree, random forest, balanced RF, weighted DT, weighted KNN.
corpus.novelty: Integrating clinical/clinicopathological data with MRI provides both preoperative diagnostic capability (parametrial invasion, lymph node metastasis) and postoperative prognostic capability (recurrence, mortality, individualized survival time) in one framework to support personalized treatment.
corpus.training_datasets: Confirmed: Overall cohort 250 cervical cancer patients from 2 tertiary hospitals (2014-2022); training set 200 patients (80%).
corpus.eval_datasets: Confirmed: held-out test set 50 patients (20%); 5-fold cross-validation on the training set; no external/cross-dataset validation reported.
corpus.evaluation_results: All claimed metrics match the source. Preoperative parametrial invasion (balanced RF): sensitivity 0.81, specificity 0.85, accuracy 0.85, F1 0.64 (confirmed). Preoperative lymph node metastasis (weighted KNN): AUC 0.72, sensitivity 0.67, specificity 0.61, accuracy 0.63, F1 0.58 (confirmed). Postoperative recurrence (weighted KNN): AUC 0.861, accuracy 0.94, sensitivity 0.80, specificity 0.96, precision 0.67, F1 0.73 (confirmed). Postoperative mortality (weighted KNN): AUC 0.765, accuracy 0.97, specificity 0.99, sensitivity 0.33 (confirmed). Survival: recurrence-free survival MAE 8.53 months, C-index 0.83 (weighted KNN, confirmed); overall survival MAE 4.36 months, C-index 0.99 (confirmed, attributed in source to regression tree (RT), not weighted KNN). The claim's value of 0.99 is correct; one extraction pass initially showed 1.0 for OS but the article body text explicitly states C-index=0.99 for the best OS model.
corpus.gaps: Only 2 tertiary centers with selection bias; only 23.2% of identified CC patients had usable MRI (external scans lacked digitalized DICOM); short follow-up (<5 years); suboptimal deep-learning performance due to small sample size; only coronal T2WI sequence used (one facet of MRI's diagnostic capability); no external validation.
corpus._evidence: "weighted KNN achieved the best performance for recurrence with the lowest MAE (8.53 mo) and highest C-index (0.83)"; "regression tree (RT) achieved the best performance for mortality (MAE=4.36 mo; C-index=0.99)"; postoperative recurrence (weighted KNN): AUC 0.861, accuracy 0.94, sensitivity 0.80, specificity 0.96, precision 0.67, F1 0.73; preoperative parametrial invasion (balanced RF): sensitivity 0.81, specificity 0.85, accuracy 0.85, F1 0.64. corpus.title: Fusion model combining ultrasound-based radiomics and deep transfer learning with clinical parameters for preoperative prediction of pelvic lymph node metastasis in cervical cancer
corpus.authors: Jihan Wang, et al.
corpus.modality: Multimodal: transvaginal B-mode ultrasound images + ultrasound radiomics + clinical/tabular parameters (max tumor diameter, RBC, WBC, alkaline phosphatase, CA125, CEA, SCC antigen)
corpus.methodology: PyRadiomics v3.0.1 extracts 1,561 handcrafted features (42 shape, 744 intensity, 775 texture); deep transfer learning with ImageNet-pretrained DenseNet121, ResNet50, AlexNet (DenseNet121 best); recursive feature elimination retaining 7 radiomic + 9 DL features; MLP (2 hidden layers, ReLU) for radiomics-DTL fusion; z-score normalization and augmentation (random crop +/-15%, flips, intensity scaling +/-20%); nomogram adds clinical parameters to the fusion model.
corpus.novelty: Stated as the first implementation of ultrasound-based radiomics-DTL fusion for cervical cancer nodal (PLNM) staging, offering a cost-effective alternative to MRI/PET-CT for resource-limited settings and quantitatively standardizing subjective ultrasound interpretation.
corpus.training_datasets: Confirmed: Training cohort 294 patients (218 PLNM-negative [74.1%], 76 PLNM-positive [25.9%]), single center (First Affiliated Hospital of Guangxi Medical University, Nanning, Guangxi, China; May 2020-Sep 2024).
corpus.eval_datasets: Confirmed: Internal testing cohort 127 patients (96 PLNM-negative [75.6%], 31 PLNM-positive [24.4%]). Total 421 patients, single center, retrospective. No external validation reported (acknowledged as a limitation).
corpus.evaluation_results: Confirmed as stated. Radiomics MLP: AUC 0.749 (train) / 0.729 (test). DTL DenseNet121: AUC 0.782 (train) / 0.702 (test). Radiomics-DTL fusion MLP: AUC 0.857 (train) / 0.753 (test), test sensitivity 0.806, specificity 0.625, ~5.1% gain over standalone DTL. Nomogram (fusion + clinical): AUC 0.871 (train) / 0.764 (test), test sensitivity 0.581, specificity 0.844.
corpus.gaps: Single-center, retrospective design with no external validation; 2D ROI ignores volumetric heterogeneity; functional ultrasound (Doppler, elastography) excluded; limited training size (n=294) may not represent population diversity; train-test AUC gap (0.871 vs 0.764) suggests potential overfitting.
corpus._evidence: "the MLP-based fusion model achieved a testing AUC of 0.753 (95% CI: 0.6494–0.8560), representing a 5.1% improvement over standalone DenseNet121." Training AUCs from tables: Radiomics MLP 0.749, DenseNet121 0.782, Fusion MLP 0.857; Nomogram 0.871 (train)/0.764 (test), test sensitivity 58.1%, specificity 84.4%.
corpus._verify_notes: Paper exists exactly as described at the claimed PMC URL (PMC12658780). Title, year (2025), and venue (Frontiers in Oncology) match. Full author list: Jihan Wang, Shengxian Bao, Tongtong Huang, Yongzhi Cai, Binbin Jin, Ji Wu (lead author Jihan Wang confirmed; "et al." accurate). All reported AUCs (train and test), sensitivity/specificity for both fusion and nomogram models, the ~5.1% fusion-over-DTL gain, MLP classifier choice, cohort sizes, PLNM class splits, center, date range, and absence of external validation all match the source. No discrepancies found.

corpus.title: An efficient framework based on large foundation model for cervical cytopathology whole slide image screening
corpus.authors: Jialong Huang, Gaojie Li, Shichao Kan et al.
corpus.venue: arXiv preprint 2407.11486; published in Biomedical Signal Processing and Control (Elsevier)
corpus.modality: Cervical cytopathology whole-slide images (WSI); also evaluated on breast fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC)
corpus.methodology: Adapts frozen large vision-language foundation models (BiomedCLIP, CLIP, PLIP) via Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) with linear adapters and SimCLR-style contrastive learning to obtain a domain-specific feature extractor; a mean-pooling-based patch filter removes low-information patches; Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) aggregators produce slide-level predictions.

FNAC 2019 is breast fine-needle aspiration cytology used to demonstrate cross-domain generalization; no separate external cervical cohort beyond the CSD held-out test set is used.

corpus.title: Classification of cervical cells from the Pap smear image using the RES_DCGAN data augmentation and ResNet50V2 with self-attention architecture
corpus.authors: Betelhem Zewdu Wubineh, Andrzej Rusiecki, Krzysztof Halawa
corpus.venue: Neural Computing and Applications, vol. 36, pp. 21801-21815 (Springer)
corpus.modality: Pap smear cervical cytology (single-cell images; Pomeranian private set and SIPaKMeD public set)
corpus.methodology: Proposes RES_DCGAN: a DCGAN with residual blocks added to the generator (improves gradient flow) to synthesize cervical cell images; generated images are mixed with real training data. Classification uses pre-trained CNNs (ResNet50V2, Xception, DenseNet121) with a self-attention layer added on top (global average pooling + dense + output). Preprocessing: resize to 224x224, rescale to (0,1), brightness/contrast adjustment, traditional augmentation (rotation, flip, translation, zoom) on real data. Generator outputs 96x96x3; FID used to assess synthetic image quality (FID 19 Pomeranian, 20 SIPaKMeD, lower than standard DCGAN). Five-fold cross-validation. Binary and multiclass scenarios on SIPaKMeD.
corpus.novelty: Improving the DCGAN architecture with residual blocks in the generator for higher-quality synthetic cervical cells to combat data scarcity/imbalance, combined with adding a self-attention mechanism on top of transfer-learning backbones to focus on important features.
corpus.training_datasets: CONFIRMED. Pomeranian Medical University (Szczecin, Poland) private set: 419 images (Table 2: HSIL 124, LSIL 61, NSIL 234), 3 classes, split 80% train / 20% test; RES_DCGAN generated 501 HSIL + 551 LSIL + 413 NSIL, giving 1800 training instances. SIPaKMeD public: 4049 images (Table 2: train 3549 / test 500), 5 classes; RES_DCGAN generated 3951 images (787 dyskeratotic, 775 koilocytotic, 807 metaplastic, 813 parabasal, 769 superficial-intermediate), giving 7500 training instances. Verbatim from source.
corpus.eval_datasets: CONFIRMED. Held-out 20% real test split of each dataset, not used for image generation: "The remaining 20% of the real testing dataset, which was not used for image generation, was used to evaluate the performance of the proposed model." No external cross-dataset validation was performed; the paper notes in its limitations that "further validation on different datasets and in real-world clinical settings is necessary to confirm the generalizability of the approach."
corpus.evaluation_results: CONFIRMED. Pomeranian (RES_DCGAN + self-attention, Table 6): Xception 98% accuracy; ResNet50V2 96.4% accuracy (precision 97.3%, recall 96.4%, F1 96.5%); DenseNet121 96.4% accuracy. SIPaKMeD (RES_DCGAN + self-attention, Table 9): DenseNet121 92% multiclass and 95% binary accuracy; ResNet50V2 86.7% multiclass and 92.4% binary accuracy. All figures match the source exactly.
corpus.gaps: Self-attention only helped ResNet50V2 and DenseNet121, not Xception; quality/realism of GAN-generated images is a limiting factor and may not perfectly replicate real cervical cell complexity; effectiveness of DCGAN images is dataset-dependent; authors state further validation on different datasets and in real clinical settings is needed; no external validation.

corpus.title: Automated Screening of Precancerous Cervical Cells Through Contrastive Self-Supervised Learning
corpus.authors: Jaewoo Chun, Ando Yu, Seokhwan Ko, Gunoh Chong, Jiyoung Park, Hyungsoo Han, Nora Jeeyoung Park, Junghwan Cho
corpus.modality: Digital liquid-based cervical cytology slides scanned at 40x; 256x256 tiles. External set is conventional Pap smear images (CRIC).
corpus.methodology: Distribution-augmented contrastive self-supervised learning (DA-SimCLR) with a ResNet18 encoder and an 8-layer MLP projection head trained with contrastive loss. Three variants: generic SimCLR, DA-SimCLR (Color) using color/hue jitter, and DA-SimCLR (Rotation). Downstream anomaly detection (one-class style) via kernel density estimation (KDE), one-class SVM, Gaussian mixture models, and K-means on learned features; t-SNE and GradCAM for interpretation. Trained only on normal (NILM) tiles. Preprocessing excludes artifacts and tiles with >50% background.
corpus.novelty: Applying distribution-augmented contrastive learning (using color augmentation specifically, since color is critical in cytopathology) to expand the training distribution and overcome the uniformity limitation of one-class normal-only training for detecting abnormal cervical cells.
corpus.training_datasets: CONFIRMED as stated: In-house 150 slides total (100 normal NILM, 50 abnormal HSIL/ASC-H); 434,442 tiles total (184,842 normal + 249,600 abnormal); upstream pretraining on 60 slides yielding 96,646 normal tiles.
corpus.eval_datasets: CONFIRMED as stated: In-house downstream test 90 slides (40 normal + 50 abnormal). Tile-level: 1,356 images per class extracted from 52 slides (26 NILM + 26 abnormal) = 2,712 tiles total; 1,586 abnormal cells annotated from the 1,356 abnormal tile images. External: CRIC dataset 400 conventional Pap smear images (1376x1020 px), 11,534 annotated cells; balanced set 2,628 normal + 2,628 abnormal tiles; 4-fold cross-validation (75% train / 25% validation per fold). Cross-dataset external validation: Yes.
corpus.evaluation_results: In-house tile-level DA-SimCLR(Color)+KDE: Precision 0.95, Recall 0.95, F1 0.95 (all ±0.05) — CONFIRMED. In-house slide-level max-aggregation AUC: DA-SimCLR(Rotation) 0.969, DA-SimCLR(Color) 0.956, SimCLR 0.947 — CONFIRMED verbatim. External CRIC DA-SimCLR(Color)+KDE: Precision 0.74, Recall 0.82, AUC 0.817 — CONFIRMED, but F1 is 0.61 (±0.03), NOT 0.78. The claimed F1 of 0.78 is the K-means value, not the KDE value (claim conflated the two rows). External CRIC DA-SimCLR(Color)+K-means: Precision 0.85, Recall 0.74, F1 0.78 — CONFIRMED.
corpus.gaps: Color-distribution sensitivity persists; lacks emphasis on cellular morphology/size/nucleus characteristics; validation data relatively small vs. training data; need multi-institutional cohorts for robust validation (performance drops notably on external CRIC set).
corpus._evidence: Table 3 KDE row, DA-SimCLR (Color): Precision 0.74 ± (0.03), Recall 0.82 ± (0.01), F1 Score 0.61 ± (0.03); text: "DA-SimCLR (Color) achieved the best AUC score with 0.817." In-house slide-level: "an AUC of 0.947 for SimCLR, 0.956 for DA-SimCLR (Color), and 0.969 for DA-SimCLR (Rotation)." Table 2 KDE DA-SimCLR (Color): Precision 0.95, Recall 0.95, F1 0.95 (±0.05).

corpus.title: DoNet: Deep De-overlapping Network for Cytology Instance Segmentation

corpus.venue: IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) 2023

corpus.methodology: DoNet uses a decompose-and-recombine strategy: a Dual-path Region segmentation Module (DRM) explicitly decomposes overlapping cell clusters into intersection and complement regions, a Semantic Consistency-guided Recombination Module (CRM) reintegrates them, and a Mask-guided Region Proposal strategy (MRP) leverages cell attention maps and the nucleus-in-cytoplasm containment relationship for inner-cell instance prediction.
corpus.novelty: Explicit de-overlapping of translucent overlapping cell clusters via decompose-and-recombine, plus exploitation of the nucleus/cytoplasm containment relationship, to resolve ambiguous boundaries and suppress mimics/debris confusion in cytology instance segmentation.
corpus.training_datasets: ISBI2014: 45 / 90 / 810 images for training / validation / testing (from the Overlapping Cervical Cytology Image Segmentation Challenge, 512x512 EDF + synthetic cervical cytology images). CPS: 137 labeled liquid-based cytology images (1000x1000; 4439 cytoplasm and 4789 nuclei annotations) evaluated via 3-fold cross-validation. (Abstract does not state splits; these are from the paper body.)
corpus.eval_datasets: ISBI2014 (Overlapping Cervical Cytology Image Segmentation Challenge) and CPS (cervical Pap smear / liquid-based cytology) datasets. Confirmed correct.

corpus.gaps: Not reported in the abstract; landmark method targeting overlapping-cluster ambiguity in cytology.
corpus._evidence: "We validate the proposed approach on ISBI2014 and CPS datasets. gapPanels.lens: Clinical translation & real-world deployment (external validation, prospective trials, regulatory, integration into pathology workflow, edge/low-resource use)

gaps.gap: External validation is the exception, not the rule: the dominant evaluation paradigm is train-and-test on the same small public benchmarks (SIPaKMeD, Herlev, Mendeley LBC), with no held-out site or scanner.
gaps.evidence: At least 15 papers explicitly report no external/cross-dataset validation: #2, #5, #6, #7, #21, #23, #24, #26, #28, #29, #30, #35, #39, #40, plus segmentation papers #13, #31 that train/test within each dataset. The headline accuracies cluster at 98-99.99% (e.g., #5 99.95%, #29/#44 99.99%, #26 99.01%, #40 98.6%), and #22 (systematic review) confirms field-wide 'overreliance on small classical public datasets without external validation' and a mean accuracy of 87.76% with range up to 100%.
gaps.why_it_matters: Near-ceiling internal numbers on tiny curated single-cell sets are not evidence of deployability; they signal optimism/overfitting. Without site-held-out validation a screening tool's true operating sensitivity/specificity on a new lab's slides is unknown, which is exactly the number a pathology service and a regulator need before adoption.

gaps.gap: When external/real-world data IS used, performance collapses, and this degradation is invisible in the majority of papers that never test it.
gaps.evidence: Concrete drops: #14 nuclei segmentation DSC 0.86->0.62 (PQ 0.86->0.25 for ViT) on the institutional WSI set; #19 (CerviPro) C-index 0.806 internal -> ~0.66 external with KM significance lost (p=0.085, p=0.211); #36 self-supervised F1 0.95 in-house -> 0.61 on external CRIC; #27 (CerviFusionNet) 0.833 internal -> 0.80 external; #11 TZ identification 83.97% -> 79.33% external; #15 CTV DSC 74.8% -> 73.4% external. #9 (Smart-CCS) shows wide prospective spread across centers (AUC 0.924 to 0.986).
gaps.why_it_matters: The recurring 10-25 point degradation from acquisition/staining/scanner differences (#14, #19, #36 all attribute it to imaging-protocol variation) means internally-validated models cannot be trusted at a new site. Papers reporting only internal metrics are systematically over-promising the clinical value that will actually be delivered.

gaps.gap: Prospective clinical evaluation and reader/workflow-impact studies are almost entirely missing; nearly all evidence is retrospective.
gaps.evidence: Only 3 of 45 report prospective data: #9 (3-center prospective AUC 0.947/0.924/0.986), #38 (prospective AUC 0.947 plus a randomized observational reader trial showing +13.3% sensitivity for AI-assisted cytopathologists), and #11 (multicenter but external validation 'limited to AI evaluation only'). The meta-analysis #37 explicitly calls for 'standardized, prospective, externally validated evaluation.' No paper reports a true RCT of patient outcomes; even #38's randomized study is observational/reader-level.
gaps.why_it_matters: Retrospective AUC does not establish that AI changes pathologist decisions, throughput, or patient outcomes in routine practice. The single human-in-the-loop study (#38) is the only one quantifying assisted-vs-unassisted reader gain, leaving the core clinical-utility question (does this catch more disease or reduce workload safely?) unanswered for the entire rest of the corpus.

gaps.gap: No engagement with regulatory requirements (FDA/CE/IVDR), quality management, or the evidentiary standards needed for a deployable diagnostic device.
gaps.evidence: Across all 45 papers there is no mention of regulatory clearance pathways, locked-model versioning, intended-use definitions, or post-market monitoring. The closest is #38 noting 'ethical/privacy considerations require ongoing monitoring.' Calibration is reported in only one paper (#4, temperature scaling); decision thresholds tied to a clinically meaningful operating point appear in only #25 and #38 (target-sensitivity operating points). Confidence intervals on the primary metric are rare (present in #8, #11, #38; absent from most single-cell papers).
gaps.why_it_matters: A screening aid is a regulated medical device. Without calibrated probabilities, pre-specified operating thresholds, CIs, and a defined intended-use/QMS framing, none of these models can move from publication to certified clinical use. The field is optimizing accuracy on benchmarks while ignoring the actual gating criteria for translation.

gaps.gap: No integration into the pathology/clinical workflow: end-to-end WSI ingestion, LIS/PACS interoperability, scanner-agnostic pipelines, and turnaround-time reporting are largely absent.
gaps.evidence: Latency/throughput is reported by only 3 papers (#1 9.75 s/WSI, #38 <120 s/WSI vs 180 s manual, #41 ~1.2 min/WSI); the rest (especially all single-cell classifiers #2,#5,#6,#7,#23,#24,#26,#39,#40) operate on pre-cropped cells, sidestepping slide detection/triage entirely. #22 flags the 'flawed assumption that cell classification alone suffices for cancer diagnosis.' No paper describes LIS/PACS hooks, vendor-neutral scanner support, or how outputs surface in a sign-out worklist. Scanner/stain robustness is named as the unsolved problem in #3, #14, #36.
gaps.why_it_matters: A model that classifies hand-cropped cells cannot screen a real slide; the hard, deployable parts are slide-level triage, abnormal-region surfacing, and fitting the cytotechnologist's sign-out workflow. Without interoperability and reported turnaround time, claimed efficiency gains are unverifiable and the tool cannot plug into an existing lab.

gaps.gap: Edge and low-resource deployment, the highest-impact setting for cervical cancer, is targeted by few papers and those underperform, with federation simulated rather than real.
gaps.evidence: Edge/federated attempts underdeliver: #17 (FL at the edge for colposcopy) reaches only 68.72% accuracy on 385 images; #32/#18 show non-IID collapse 94.36%->78.4%; the FL review #3 reports lack of testing under client dropout and extreme heterogeneity, and that only 2/24 studies even named their FL framework. 'Lightweight' models (#23 MaxCerVixT, #24 CCanNet, #31 distillation) report parameter counts but no on-device latency, memory, or low-end-hardware/offline benchmarks. #32's federation is on lab-curated public sets (simulated, not real multi-institution).
gaps.why_it_matters: Most cervical cancer mortality is in low-resource regions where colposcopy/cytology and connectivity are scarce, so robust offline/edge inference and privacy-preserving cross-site training are the translation bottleneck. The corpus shows these approaches either lose substantial accuracy (real heterogeneity, #17/#32) or only demonstrate parameter savings without proving they run on accessible field hardware.

gaps.gap: Datasets are demographically narrow and single-institution, with no reporting of subgroup performance, undermining generalizability and equity claims for deployment.
gaps.evidence: Single-center/single-country sourcing and limited diversity are flagged repeatedly: #4 (single IARC source), #6 ('limited demographic representation'), #16 (expert opinions from a single country), #20/#28/#21/#34 (single-center), #27/#34 (single-institution self-built, HPV-positive cohort). #20 notes only 23.2% of patients had usable DICOM (selection bias). No paper reports stratified performance by age, ethnicity, HPV status, or scanner vendor.
gaps.why_it_matters: A model validated on one population/one device can silently fail or be inequitable across the diverse populations a national screening program serves. Absence of subgroup metrics means deployment risk (e.g., reduced sensitivity in an underrepresented group) is unmeasured, which is both a clinical-safety and a regulatory-equity gap.

gaps.gap: Lack of reproducibility infrastructure (public code, open clinical datasets, standardized protocols) blocks independent external validation and head-to-head benchmarking needed for translation.
gaps.evidence: Multiple papers explicitly note 'no public code' or unavailable data: #8 (no public code), #34/#27 (datasets not public/privacy), #1/#9 needing multi-institutional validation. The two systematic reviews #3 and #22 both identify the absence of standardized evaluation protocols, inconsistent reporting/diagnostic criteria, and under-reporting of frameworks as field-wide problems. Metrics are inconsistent (#22: 93.9% report accuracy but few report F1/PR-AUC; many single-cell papers omit CIs).
gaps.why_it_matters: Without shared code, common clinical-grade test sets, and harmonized metrics/operating points, claims cannot be independently externally validated and labs cannot compare candidate tools on equal footing, exactly the prerequisites for evidence-based procurement and regulatory submission.

gapPanels.lens: Technical / ML methodology (architectures, knowledge distillation, transformers, calibration, reproducibility, overfitting, benchmarking rigor)

gaps.gap: Near-ceiling accuracy on small public single-cell benchmarks (SIPaKMeD/Herlev) with no external/cross-dataset validation is the dominant evaluation pattern, masking overfitting and benchmark saturation
gaps.evidence: A large block of papers report 98-100% on the same two-to-three public datasets while explicitly lacking external validation: #2 (Swin 99.27% Herlev/98.82% SIPaKMeD), #5 (99.95% SIPaKMeD 2-class), #6 (CICNN 99.14%), #7 (99.18% SIPaKMeD), #23 (MaxCerVixT 99.02%), #24 (CCanNet 98.53%), #26 (Swin-GA-RF 99.01%), #39 (CerviFormer), #40 (CerviXpert 98.6%). The systematic reviews #22 and #37 confirm this field-wide: #22 finds mean accuracy 87.76% with range up to 100%, 93.9% of studies reporting only accuracy, and overreliance on small classical public datasets without external validation; #37 calls for standardized, prospective, externally validated evaluation.
gaps.why_it_matters: SIPaKMeD/Herlev are small, lab-curated, pre-cropped single-cell sets; 99%+ scores are no longer discriminative between methods and do not predict performance on real slides. Papers that DID test cross-domain show large drops (#14 institutional WSI Dice falls from 0.86 to 0.62; #36 external CRIC F1 collapses from 0.95 to 0.61; #32 non-IID accuracy drops 94.4% to 78.4%), proving the in-distribution numbers are over-optimistic. Without held-out external cohorts the reported gains are not clinically meaningful.

gaps.gap: Data-leakage and over-optimism from oversampling/augmentation applied before splitting, especially on tabular risk-factor data, producing implausible ~99.99% scores
gaps.evidence: Tabular UCI/Kaggle risk-factor papers report essentially perfect metrics after SMOTE/ADASYN/imputation + ensembling: #29 (voting classifier 99.99% acc/prec/rec/F1; un-augmented baseline only 80.13%), #44 (VC XGB+RF+ETC 99.99%), #16 (SRXL 0.98 acc with SMOTE), #30 (DT 97.6%). The verifications for #29 and #44 explicitly flag possible data-leakage/over-optimism from synthetic oversampling plus CNN-feature augmentation. The jump from ~80% (raw) to ~99.99% (augmented) in #29 is the tell-tale signature.
gaps.why_it_matters: When SMOTE/feature-augmentation is run on the full dataset before train/test partition, synthetic neighbors of test points leak into training, inflating metrics toward 100%. These models would not generalize to a real screening population, and the practice contaminates the literature's reported state-of-the-art. Correct protocol (resample inside CV folds only) is not demonstrated.

gaps.gap: Probability calibration is essentially absent despite the diagnostic/risk-stratification use case; only one paper reports calibration
gaps.evidence: Across 45 papers, only #4 (TopotiCerv) reports calibrated probabilities (temperature scaling) and Cohen's kappa/MCC together. The vast majority report only accuracy/AUC/F1 with no reliability diagrams, ECE, Brier score, or post-hoc calibration. #22's review confirms 93.9% of studies report accuracy as the primary metric and reporting is inconsistent; MCC/PR-AUC are rarely reported (#2 only partially, and Herlev MCC/PR-AUC were unreadable). Prognostic models (#19, #20, #28, #45) report C-index/AUC but no calibration curves for the predicted survival probabilities.
gaps.why_it_matters: Screening and triage decisions depend on trustworthy probability thresholds (e.g., ASC-US+/HSIL+ operating points). Uncalibrated softmax outputs from transformers/CNNs are typically over-confident, so threshold selection and clinician trust break down at deployment. Lack of calibration also makes the near-ceiling AUCs unverifiable as decision-ready.

gaps.gap: Pervasive train-vs-test and internal-vs-external performance gaps signal overfitting, but are rarely quantified, regularized against, or treated as the headline result
gaps.evidence: Where external/holdout numbers exist, the gap is large and under-discussed: #21 (train AUC 0.871 vs test 0.764, verification flags overfitting), #45 (training AUC 0.987/validation 0.989 vs test 0.819 with specificity/precision = 1.000 in train, a classic overfit signature), #19 (training-cohort AUC 0.96/0.92/0.87 vs external 0.64/0.63, KM non-significant externally), #20 (suboptimal DL attributed to small sample). Segmentation shows the same: #14 (CNseg-trained model crashes on institutional WSIs). Smart-CCS (#9) is a rare positive counter-example with test-time adaptation and explicit prospective AUCs 0.947-0.986.
gaps.why_it_matters: Reporting only the best (internal/training) number is misleading; the external delta is the real measure of clinical readiness. Few papers employ or report regularization, domain adaptation, or test-time adaptation to close the gap, so models that look state-of-the-art are brittle to scanner/stain/population shift, the exact conditions of real screening programs.

gaps.gap: Reproducibility infrastructure is missing: no public code, undisclosed dataset sizes/splits, private single-institution datasets, and under-reported frameworks/hyperparameters
gaps.evidence: Multiple verifications note 'no public code' (#6, #8, #31), private non-shared datasets (#27, #34, #41 717-sample private set), and undisclosed dataset size/splits (#4 size/split not reported, #7 sizes not detailed, #2 exact sizes unreadable). #34 is a documented misattribution where headline metrics belonged to a different paper. The FL reviews #3 and #18 find only 2 of 24 studies reported their FL framework and full texts are closed-access; #17/#18 had metrics that were claimed 'not reported' but were actually present, indicating poor primary-source transparency.
gaps.why_it_matters: Without code, exact splits, seeds, and dataset provenance, the headline metrics cannot be reproduced or fairly compared, and the misattribution in #34 shows the literature already contains propagated errors. This undermines benchmarking rigor across the whole field and makes meta-analysis (#22, #37) note heterogeneity and inconsistent reporting as primary limitations.

gaps.gap: Weak benchmarking rigor: no statistical comparison (CIs, significance tests, multiple seeds) between competing architectures, and no shared protocol so cross-paper numbers are not comparable
gaps.evidence: Most classification papers report single point estimates without confidence intervals or significance testing against baselines (#2, #5, #7, #23, #24, #26, #40). Where CIs/seeds appear it is the exception (#8 AUROC with 95% CI; #43/#45 report ±std over folds). Architecture 'wins' are claimed on sub-1% accuracy differences that fall within noise (#31 claims 0.8-2% gains; #24 CCanNet 98.53% vs Swin 96.57% with no significance test). Reviews #22 and #37 explicitly cite inconsistent diagnostic criteria, limited cross-validation, and lack of standardized evaluation protocols.
gaps.why_it_matters: Claiming a new transformer/hybrid is superior based on a fraction-of-a-percent gap on a saturated benchmark, single seed, and no significance test is statistically unsound. Without a shared task definition (class taxonomy varies: 2/3/5/7-class) and protocol, the dozens of 98-99% results cannot be ranked, so genuine architectural progress is indistinguishable from tuning/dataset luck.

gaps.gap: Knowledge distillation and lightweight/efficient design are claimed but under-validated: efficiency-accuracy trade-offs, FLOPs/parameter reductions, and student-vs-teacher fidelity are largely unmeasured
gaps.evidence: Distillation/lightweight papers report accuracy but omit the efficiency evidence that justifies them: #31 (CerviSegNet-DistillPlus) verification notes exact parameter/FLOPs reduction from pruning is not stated; #24 (CCanNet) reports parameter count but the verification notes the architecture is 'still relatively complex'; #23 (MaxCerVixT 'lightweight ViT') gives no latency/FLOPs in the accessed record. Only a few report runtime (#1 9.75 s/WSI, #38 <120 s/WSI, #41 ~1.2 min). No distillation paper reports teacher-vs-student gap, calibration drift under distillation, or on-device latency.
gaps.why_it_matters: The clinical selling point of distilled/lightweight models is deployability at the edge or high-throughput WSI screening, yet without FLOPs, parameter counts, memory, and latency on target hardware, plus the accuracy retained relative to the teacher, the 'efficiency' claim is unsubstantiated. #17's edge-FL result (68.72% accuracy) shows real edge performance can be far below the lab numbers.

gaps.gap: Transformer/MIL architectures are adopted for cell- or patch-level tasks without modeling spatial/slide context, and modern MIL baselines are frequently missing from comparisons
gaps.evidence: #8 explicitly uses TF-IDF over patches which ignores spatial relations and does NOT compare against modern MIL (CLAM, TransMIL) despite being a WSI subtyping paper. Many 'WSI' or 'screening' claims are actually single-cell/tile classification reframed (#22 review flags the 'flawed assumption that cell classification alone suffices for cancer diagnosis'; #26 notes cell-level classification misses tissue-level complexity). Where MIL is used it is sometimes only a vanilla baseline (#42 reports relative +11.11% over vanilla MIL but no absolute AUC/kappa and no strong MIL comparator).
gaps.why_it_matters: Cancer diagnosis depends on slide-level spatial context and rare-event detection; bag-of-patches/TF-IDF and single-cell pipelines discard the spatial arrangement that pathologists use. Omitting CLAM/TransMIL/DSMIL baselines means new aggregators are not benchmarked against the genuine state of the art, so reported slide-level gains may not hold against proper MIL.

gaps.gap: GAN/synthetic-data augmentation and self-supervised pretraining are used to inflate small datasets without validating that synthetic samples preserve diagnostic morphology or avoid distribution leakage
gaps.evidence: #35 (RES_DCGAN) verification notes GAN image realism is a limiting factor that may not replicate real cervical-cell complexity and helped only some backbones; #41 (CervixFormer) uses SAGAN synthesis adding pipeline complexity. Self-supervised #36 (DA-SimCLR) shows strong in-house but external CRIC drop (F1 0.95 to 0.61) tied to color-distribution sensitivity. No paper reports a quantitative fidelity/diversity metric (e.g., FID) for generated cells or a leakage check that synthetic samples derived from test images don't enter training.
gaps.why_it_matters: If GAN samples are low-fidelity they teach the model artifacts; if they are too faithful to specific real images they cause leakage and over-optimism. Without fidelity metrics and a clean separation, augmentation-driven accuracy gains (a common claim) cannot be trusted, and the model may learn staining/color shortcuts rather than morphology, exactly the failure observed externally in #36.

gapPanels.lens: Data, datasets & generalization (dataset size/diversity, class imbalance, domain/scanner shift, cross-dataset validation, multimodal fusion, privacy/federated, annotation quality)

gaps.gap: Near-total absence of true held-out external / cross-dataset validation, even in papers that touch multiple datasets
gaps.evidence: Explicitly 'no external validation' in papers 2, 5, 6, 7, 10, 16, 21, 24, 26, 28, 29, 30, 39, 40, 44, 45. Critically, several 'multi-dataset' papers only train AND test within each dataset rather than holding one out: paper 31 (CerviSegNet-DistillPlus) trains/tests within Cx22, Herlev, SIPaKMeD separately; review 22 names 'overreliance on small classical public datasets without external validation' as a field pattern; review 37 calls for 'standardized, prospective, externally validated evaluation.' The handful that DO test externally show the cost of skipping it (papers 9, 11, 14, 19, 27, 36).
gaps.why_it_matters: Internal-only metrics (frequently 98-99.99%) are not evidence of clinical readiness. Without a held-out external cohort, reported accuracy is an upper bound that consistently fails to transfer (see the domain-shift gap), so the literature systematically overstates deployable performance and cannot rank methods against each other.

gaps.gap: Documented, severe performance collapse under domain / scanner / staining / site shift that most papers never measure
gaps.evidence: Where external testing is actually done, drops are large and concrete: paper 14 nuclei segmentation DSC 0.89->0.62 (IoU 0.82->0.45) on institutional WSIs vs ISBI; paper 36 SSL precision/recall/F1 0.95 in-house -> external CRIC F1 0.61 and AUC 0.817; paper 19 (CerviPro) prognosis AUC ~0.96 internal -> ~0.64 external (KM non-significant) until transfer-learning re-tuning; papers 32 and 18 both drop 94.36% (IID) -> ~78.4% (non-IID); paper 11 TZ classification 83.97% internal -> 79.33% external. Causes named: image-acquisition differences, blur/z-stacking artifacts (14), color-distribution sensitivity (36), staining/hardware variability across sites (review 3), imaging-protocol variation (19).
gaps.why_it_matters: Cervical screening AI must run across many scanners, stain batches, and clinics (especially low-resource settings). A 20-30 point drop turns a 'screening-grade' model into one that misses cancers or floods clinicians with false positives. The field largely does not quantify this, so robustness is unknown for nearly every model that reports only in-distribution numbers.

gaps.gap: Monoculture of small, lab-curated single-cell public datasets (SIPaKMeD, Herlev, Mendeley LBC) standing in for whole-slide clinical reality
gaps.evidence: SIPaKMeD and/or Herlev are the sole or primary benchmark in papers 2, 5, 6, 7, 23, 24, 26, 35, 39, 40 (plus tabular UCI monoculture in 16, 29, 30, 44). Review 22 explicitly flags 'overreliance on small classical public datasets' and the 'flawed assumption that cell classification alone suffices for cancer diagnosis.' Datasets are tiny: paper 8 ~438 WSIs, paper 13 ISBI2015 only 8 training images, paper 17 385 images, paper 41 717 samples, paper 21 n=294, paper 20 a single small Kaggle set.
gaps.why_it_matters: Pre-segmented, clean, balanced single cells do not represent WSIs with overlapping cells, debris, inflammation, and rare entities. Models tuned to these benchmarks learn dataset-specific shortcuts (hence 99% accuracies that don't transfer), and segmentation/detection of overlapping cells in dense regions, the actual clinical bottleneck, remains unsolved (papers 13, 43 target exactly this and still fail in densest regions).

gaps.gap: Class imbalance and rare-class coverage handled superficially, with oversampling that risks data leakage rather than genuine minority-class learning
gaps.evidence: Tabular UCI papers apply SMOTE/ADASYN/KNN-imputation and then report 99.99% (papers 29, 44) or 0.98-0.995 AUC (16, 30) — the verifier notes explicit 'possible data-leakage/over-optimism' concerns in 29 and 44, and low 80% specificity in 30. On the imaging side, rare but lethal classes are simply absent: paper 8 cannot identify neuroendocrine/mesenchymal subtypes (only 2 subtypes); paper 38 had too few SCC samples to form a WSI category; review 22 notes 'inconsistent diagnostic criteria.' Few papers report PR-AUC/MCC (only 2, 16) despite imbalance.
gaps.why_it_matters: Cervical cancer screening is an extreme-imbalance problem (few positives among many normals) where the minority class is the clinically decisive one. Oversampling-before-split inflates metrics without improving minority detection, and missing rare aggressive subtypes (neuroendocrine, adenocarcinoma variants, SCC) means the most dangerous cases are exactly what these models are not validated to catch.

gaps.gap: Multimodal fusion is brittle and unvalidated across sites, and depends on complete, matched, co-registered modalities that are rarely available in practice
gaps.evidence: Fusion papers report near-ceiling internal numbers but no external validation and/or strict data requirements: paper 4 (TopotiCerv) AUC ~0.999 on a single IARC source, no cross-dataset test, requires matched structured clinical variables; paper 34 single-institution (Fudan), no external validation, and the verifier found a metric misattribution in the literature; paper 20 (MRI+clinicopathology) only 23.2% of patients had usable digitalized DICOM and used a single MRI sequence; papers 19, 21, 28, 45 are single-/two-center with no external validation and acknowledge missing modalities (no Doppler/elastography in 21, no multiparametric MRI fusion in 28, imaging-only with no tumor markers in 45). Paper 27 needs an HPV-positive cohort and acetic-acid time series.
gaps.why_it_matters: Fusion gains evaporate when a modality is missing, mis-registered, or acquired on a different protocol — exactly the norm across clinics. AUC ~0.999 on one source signals overfitting to that source's joint distribution, not a generalizable multimodal model. Robust missing-modality handling and multi-center fusion validation are absent, so reported fusion benefits are not yet trustworthy for deployment.

gaps.gap: Federated / privacy-preserving training is nascent, mostly simulated, and demonstrably fragile under realistic heterogeneity
gaps.evidence: Only papers 3, 17, 18, 32, 33 engage FL. Review 3 finds across 24 studies that standardized protocols are lacking, FL frameworks are under-reported (only 2 of 24 named one), and testing under 'extreme heterogeneity and client dropout' is insufficient. Real heterogeneity breaks performance: papers 18 and 32 both fall 94.36% (IID) -> ~78.4% (non-IID). Paper 32 uses simulated rather than real multi-institution federation with no differential privacy or secure aggregation; paper 17 uses only 385 images across few sites at 68.72% accuracy. Only paper 33 (FedDP) reports differential privacy (epsilon=0.5), and only at a single privacy budget.
gaps.why_it_matters: Federated learning is the main credible path to large, diverse, privacy-compliant cervical datasets across institutions and countries. But current work is simulated on the same small public sets, collapses under the non-IID conditions that define real multi-site data, and almost never combines privacy guarantees with client dropout/heterogeneity testing — so the privacy-vs-utility-vs-robustness trade-off needed for actual multi-hospital deployment is unquantified.

gaps.gap: Annotation quality, inter-observer variability, and ground-truth provenance are largely unaddressed, with reliance on synthetic or cytology-only labels
gaps.evidence: Paper 1 (UniCAS) is cytology-label-only with 'no histopathological gold-standard validation'; paper 11 'lacks an absolute subjective gold standard'; paper 15 had delineation by a single senior oncologist (no inter-observer analysis); paper 28 reports inter-observer DSC 0.896/0.867 but is single-center; paper 13 relies on synthetic ISBI2014 images; papers 35 and 41 lean on GAN-synthesized data (RES_DCGAN, SAGAN) whose realism is flagged as a limiting factor. Review 22 cites 'inconsistent diagnostic criteria' and review 3 notes annotation/staining variability across sites.
gaps.why_it_matters: Models are only as good as their labels. Cytology-only or single-reader ground truth bakes in label noise and observer bias that no amount of model capacity fixes, and training/evaluating on synthetic cells risks learning artifacts rather than pathology. Without histopathology-confirmed, multi-reader, provenance-tracked labels, reported accuracies cannot be interpreted as agreement with clinical truth.

gaps.gap: Lack of demographic, geographic, and population diversity reporting, undermining equity and generalizability claims
gaps.evidence: Papers explicitly flag narrow representation: paper 6 'limited demographic representation limiting generalizability'; paper 16 expert knowledge and data from a single country with 'resource constraints limited geographic diversity'; paper 5 'lack of dataset diversity limiting generalizability'; review 22 notes 'reduced clinical representativeness of datasets'; paper 10 authors call for 'evaluation across diverse populations'; paper 20 has selection bias from 2 tertiary centers. Most papers do not report patient demographics, HPV-genotype distribution, or source geography at all.
gaps.why_it_matters: Cervical cancer burden is concentrated in low- and middle-income populations underrepresented in these datasets (which skew to a few institutions/countries). Models validated on narrow demographics may underperform precisely where screening is most needed, and the near-universal failure to even report population composition makes it impossible to assess fairness or external applicability.

themes.theme: External / cross-site validation as the default, not the exception
themes.gap: The dominant evaluation paradigm is train-and-test on the same small public single-cell benchmarks (SIPaKMeD, Herlev, Mendeley LBC) with no held-out site, scanner, or external cohort. Internal-only metrics (98-99.99%) are reported as if they were deployable performance, so methods cannot be ranked against each other and the literature systematically overstates clinical readiness.
themes.evidence: All three lenses independently flag near-total absence of held-out external validation. The few papers that do test cross-domain show large collapses: institutional WSI Dice 0.86->0.62 (#14), external CRIC F1 0.95->0.61 (#36), non-IID accuracy 94.4%->78.4% (#32). Near-ceiling scores on saturated benchmarks no longer discriminate between methods.
themes.opportunity: Establish a mandatory leave-one-site-out / external-cohort validation protocol and a shared multi-institution, multi-scanner clinical-grade benchmark with fixed splits, seeds, and reported operating points. Make the internal-vs-external delta (not the best internal number) the headline metric, with CIs and significance tests across multiple seeds and across the varying 2/3/5/7-class taxonomies.

themes.theme: Domain / scanner / stain / population shift robustness
themes.gap: A documented, severe (10-30 point) performance collapse under acquisition, staining, scanner, and site variation that the vast majority of papers never measure, let alone mitigate. Domain adaptation, test-time adaptation, stain normalization, and regularization against the external gap are rarely employed or reported.
themes.evidence: Lenses 1, 2, and 3 all attribute a recurring 10-25/20-30 point degradation to imaging-protocol variation (#14, #19, #36). The external F1 collapse in #36 is explicitly linked to models learning staining/color shortcuts rather than morphology.
themes.opportunity: Treat shift robustness as a first-class objective: benchmark stain-normalization, domain-generalization, and test-time-adaptation methods specifically on cervical cytology/WSI under controlled scanner/stain perturbations; report robustness curves (accuracy vs. simulated and real shift) rather than a single point; and quantify whether models rely on morphology vs. color shortcuts via targeted stain-invariance probes.

themes.theme: Dataset monoculture vs. whole-slide clinical reality
themes.gap: Small, lab-curated, pre-segmented, balanced single-cell datasets stand in for whole-slide reality. The actual clinical bottlenecks (segmentation/detection of overlapping cells in dense regions, debris, inflammation, slide-level triage) remain unsolved, and rare aggressive subtypes are absent.
themes.evidence: Lens 3 notes papers 13 and 43 target overlapping-cell segmentation and still fail in the densest regions. Single-cell pipelines discard the spatial arrangement pathologists use, and 99% accuracies are tied to dataset-specific shortcuts that do not transfer.
themes.opportunity: Curate and release WSI-level cervical datasets with region/cell annotations covering overlapping clusters, debris, inflammation, and rare entities (neuroendocrine, adenocarcinoma variants, SCC). Reframe the task from clean single-cell classification to slide-level triage + abnormal-region surfacing, and benchmark dense-region overlapping-cell segmentation as a named, hard subtask.

themes.theme: Slide-level spatial context and rare-event detection (MIL done properly)
themes.gap: Cancer diagnosis depends on slide-level spatial context and rare-event detection, yet transformer/MIL aggregators are adopted at cell/patch level without modeling spatial arrangement, and strong modern MIL baselines are routinely omitted from comparisons.
themes.evidence: Lens 2 notes bag-of-patches/TF-IDF and single-cell pipelines discard spatial arrangement, and that CLAM/TransMIL/DSMIL baselines are frequently missing, so claimed slide-level gains may not hold against proper MIL.
themes.opportunity: Build and benchmark spatially-aware slide-level pipelines against the genuine MIL state of the art (CLAM, TransMIL, DSMIL) on whole slides, with explicit evaluation of rare-positive detection (sensitivity at fixed low false-positive rates) rather than balanced-set accuracy.

themes.theme: Calibration, decision-readiness, and clinical operating points
themes.gap: Probability calibration is essentially absent (only one paper reports it) despite the screening/triage use case, which depends on trustworthy thresholds (ASC-US+/HSIL+). Uncalibrated, over-confident outputs make threshold selection and clinician trust break down at deployment, and make headline AUCs unverifiable as decision-ready.
themes.evidence: Lens 1 and Lens 2 both flag missing calibration, pre-specified operating thresholds, and CIs as gating criteria the field ignores while optimizing benchmark accuracy.
themes.opportunity: Report calibration (reliability diagrams, ECE) and pre-specified, externally-validated operating thresholds tied to clinical decision points (ASC-US+/HSIL+) with confidence intervals; evaluate post-hoc calibration and conformal prediction for screening, and report sensitivity/specificity at the chosen threshold on external data, not just AUC.

themes.theme: Data leakage, benchmarking rigor, and reproducibility
themes.gap: Over-optimism from oversampling/augmentation applied before splitting (implausible ~99.99% scores, especially on tabular risk-factor data); no statistical comparison (CIs, significance, multiple seeds); no shared task/protocol; and missing reproducibility infrastructure (no public code, undisclosed splits/sizes, private single-institution data, propagated misattributions).
themes.evidence: Lens 2 details SMOTE-before-split leakage and a propagated error (#34); meta-analyses (#22, #37) cite heterogeneity and inconsistent reporting as primary limitations. Lenses 1 and 3 echo the reproducibility/standardization gap as a blocker for external validation and procurement.
themes.opportunity: Adopt and police leakage-safe protocols (resample strictly inside CV folds), mandatory code/seed/split release, a standardized class taxonomy and metric set, and statistical comparison across seeds. A community reproducibility checklist plus a curated, leakage-audited leaderboard would let labs do head-to-head, evidence-based comparison.

themes.theme: Validated efficiency for edge / low-resource deployment
themes.gap: Knowledge distillation and lightweight design are claimed but under-validated: FLOPs, parameter counts, memory, latency on target field hardware, and student-vs-teacher fidelity are largely unmeasured. The highest-impact setting (low-resource regions) is targeted by few papers, and those underperform.
themes.evidence: Lens 2 notes efficiency claims lack hardware metrics; Lens 1 notes edge/low-resource work is scarce and degraded. #17's edge-FL result (68.72% accuracy) shows real edge performance far below lab numbers.
themes.opportunity: Require deployment-grade efficiency reporting: accuracy retained vs. teacher, plus FLOPs/params/memory/latency benchmarked on accessible field hardware (e.g., low-cost microscope-attached devices, mobile/Raspberry-class compute) under realistic throughput. Co-design distilled models for offline inference and report the accuracy-cost frontier against the deployment constraint, not just parameter savings.

themes.theme: Federated / privacy-preserving training under realistic heterogeneity
themes.gap: Federated learning is the main credible path to large, diverse, privacy-compliant cervical datasets, but current work is mostly simulated on the same small public sets, collapses under non-IID conditions, and rarely combines privacy guarantees with client-dropout/heterogeneity testing. The privacy-vs-utility-vs-robustness trade-off is unquantified.
themes.evidence: Lenses 1, 2, and 3 all flag federation as simulated rather than real; #32 shows non-IID accuracy dropping 94.4%->78.4%; #17 edge-FL at 68.72%.
themes.opportunity: Run real (or rigorously non-IID-simulated) multi-institution federated studies that jointly report privacy budget (e.g., differential-privacy epsilon), client dropout/heterogeneity robustness, and external accuracy, charting the privacy-utility-robustness frontier needed for genuine multi-hospital, multi-country deployment.

themes.theme: Annotation quality, ground-truth provenance, and label noise
themes.gap: Annotation quality, inter-observer variability, and ground-truth provenance are largely unaddressed; reliance on cytology-only, single-reader, or synthetic labels bakes in observer bias and label noise that model capacity cannot fix, and makes reported accuracies uninterpretable as agreement with clinical truth.
themes.evidence: Lens 3 specifies the need for histopathology-confirmed, multi-reader, provenance-tracked labels and warns that training/evaluating on synthetic cells risks learning artifacts.
themes.opportunity: Build datasets with histopathology-confirmed, multi-reader ground truth and report inter-observer agreement; develop and evaluate label-noise-robust training; and benchmark models against the ceiling of human inter-reader variability rather than against potentially noisy single-reader labels.

themes.theme: Trustworthy synthetic data and self-supervised pretraining
themes.gap: GAN/synthetic augmentation and self-supervised pretraining are used to inflate small datasets without validating that synthetic samples preserve diagnostic morphology or avoid distribution leakage; low-fidelity samples teach artifacts, over-faithful ones cause leakage, and color/stain shortcuts get learned.
themes.evidence: Lens 2 links unvalidated augmentation to the external failure observed in #36 (color shortcuts over morphology); Lens 3 echoes the synthetic-label risk.
themes.opportunity: Require fidelity and diversity metrics for synthetic data, a strict clean separation between synthetic-source images and the real test set (leakage audit), and ablations isolating the contribution of synthetic/self-supervised pretraining; verify morphology preservation via pathologist review or morphology-targeted metrics rather than downstream accuracy alone.

themes.theme: Robust multimodal fusion under missing/mismatched modalities
themes.gap: Multimodal fusion is brittle and unvalidated across sites and depends on complete, matched, co-registered modalities rarely available in practice; gains evaporate when a modality is missing or mis-registered, and near-perfect single-source AUC (~0.999) signals joint-distribution overfitting.
themes.evidence: Lens 3 flags absent missing-modality handling and absent multi-center fusion validation.
themes.opportunity: Develop and benchmark fusion models with explicit missing-modality and mis-registration robustness (modality dropout at train/test time), validate on multi-center data with realistic modality availability, and report performance degradation curves as modalities are removed rather than only the all-modalities-present number.

themes.theme: Prospective clinical utility, workflow integration, and regulatory readiness
themes.gap: Prospective evaluation, reader/workflow-impact studies, end-to-end WSI ingestion, LIS/PACS interoperability, scanner-agnostic pipelines, turnaround-time reporting, and engagement with regulatory/QMS evidentiary standards (FDA/CE/IVDR) are almost entirely absent. Demographic/geographic diversity and subgroup performance are unreported, undermining equity and regulatory-fairness claims.
themes.evidence: Lens 1 notes the single human-in-the-loop study (#38) is the only assisted-vs-unassisted reader gain; nearly all evidence is retrospective; models classify hand-cropped cells rather than screening real slides; subgroup metrics and population composition are near-universally unreported.
themes.opportunity: Run prospective, reader-in-the-loop studies measuring assisted-vs-unassisted sensitivity/specificity, throughput, and turnaround time; build end-to-end slide-to-sign-out pipelines with LIS/PACS interoperability; and frame work around an intended-use/QMS/regulatory template including pre-specified thresholds, CIs, calibration, and mandatory subgroup (demographic/geographic) performance reporting for equity.

top_opportunities: Create and release a shared, multi-institution, multi-scanner WSI-level cervical benchmark with fixed splits/seeds, a standardized class taxonomy, histopathology-confirmed multi-reader labels, and a leakage-audited public leaderboard. This single artifact unblocks external validation, fair head-to-head benchmarking, and procurement-grade comparison, the prerequisite gap shared by all three lenses.

Make leave-one-site-out external validation plus the internal-vs-external delta the mandatory headline result, reported with calibration (reliability/ECE), pre-specified clinical operating thresholds (ASC-US+/HSIL+), CIs, and significance across multiple seeds, replacing saturated single-number internal accuracy.

Reframe the core task from clean single-cell classification to slide-level triage and abnormal-region surfacing with spatial context, benchmarked against proper modern MIL baselines (CLAM/TransMIL/DSMIL) and evaluated on rare-positive sensitivity at fixed low false-positive rates.

Deliver validated, deployment-grade efficiency for low-resource/edge settings: report accuracy-retained-vs-teacher alongside FLOPs/params/memory/latency on accessible field hardware under realistic throughput and offline operation, turning unsubstantiated 'lightweight' claims into a measured accuracy-cost frontier.

Run real (or rigorously non-IID) multi-site federated studies that jointly quantify the privacy (DP epsilon)-utility-robustness (client dropout/heterogeneity) frontier on external cohorts, moving federation from simulated-on-toy-data to a credible path for large diverse private datasets.

Establish robustness-to-shift as a first-class, reported objective: benchmark stain normalization, domain generalization, and test-time adaptation under controlled scanner/stain perturbations, with morphology-vs-color-shortcut probes and accuracy-vs-shift robustness curves.

Audit and stamp out data leakage (resample strictly inside CV folds; validate synthetic-data fidelity and enforce synthetic/test separation) and adopt a community reproducibility checklist mandating public code, seeds, splits, and dataset provenance.

Conduct prospective, reader-in-the-loop clinical-utility and workflow-impact studies (assisted-vs-unassisted sensitivity, throughput, turnaround time) within an end-to-end LIS/PACS-interoperable, regulatory/QMS-framed pipeline that reports mandatory demographic subgroup performance for equity.
